static.topic: India–US Relations and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World; bilateral relations
static.whatIsIt: India and the United States maintain a broad strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology, energy and diaspora links, while India retains strategic autonomy and multi-alignment across the Quad, BRICS, SCO and G20.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954); post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with Washington. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017. India held the G20 presidency in 2022–23.
static.geography: Indo-Pacific and the Indian Ocean Region
static.socioEconomic: Large Indian diaspora and Indian-American political presence; growing goods, services and technology trade; defence-industrial co-production.
static.whyInNews: US midterm results can alter the composition of Congress and hence the political tone of trade, immigration (including H-1B) and defence-industrial cooperation with India.
static.wayForward: Sustain issue-based engagement across administrations, deepen defence-industrial co-production and critical-technology ties, while preserving strategic autonomy and multi-alignment.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
Quad members: India, the United States, Japan and Australia; the grouping was revived at senior-official level in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: How do shifts in US domestic politics affect India's pursuit of strategic autonomy? Examine with reference to trade, technology and defence ties.

static.topic: Comparative Federalism: US and Indian Models
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: The US is a classical federation with enumerated federal powers and residual powers left to the states; India is a quasi-federal union where powers are divided by the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule) and residuary powers rest with the Union (Art. 248).
static.background: In India, the Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined the Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.whyInNews: US midterms elect state governors and state legislatures alongside Congress, illustrating how federal and state competences are separated in a classical federation.
static.wayForward: Use comparative federalism to evaluate India's cooperative and competitive federalism instruments such as the GST Council, NITI Aayog and the Inter-State Council.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for the President's assent (Art. 254).
The Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the US and Indian federal schemes on residuary powers and intergovernmental dispute resolution, and assess cooperative federalism in practice.

static.topic: US Congress and the Legislative Process
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process (comparative legislatures)
static.whatIsIt: The US Congress is bicameral: the House of Representatives has 435 seats with two-year terms, and the Senate has 100 seats with six-year staggered terms, about one-third contested every two years. A Bill requires passage in both chambers and presidential approval, with a veto override needing a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
static.background: Midterm elections are held midway through a presidential term and historically cost the President's party seats. The Mississippi Senate seat was held by Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who was appointed in 2018 and subsequently elected in 2020.
static.whyInNews: The 2026 midterms involved all 435 House seats, 35 of the 100 Senate seats and governorships in 36 states, with about 210 million registered voters.
prelimsPointers: All 435 House seats are contested every two years; senators serve six-year terms, with roughly one-third of seats up each cycle.
A presidential veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the US Congress and the Indian Parliament on bicameralism, money bills and mechanisms of executive accountability.

static.topic: Visa, entry and deportation regime for foreigners in India
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Government Policies & Interventions; Union Government and administration; International Relations (visa and travel regimes)
static.whatIsIt: The legal framework that governs how foreigners enter, stay in and leave India. A visa issued by an Indian mission abroad is a permission to travel to India, not an enforceable right to enter; a competent authority can cancel a visa or refuse entry at the port of arrival.
static.background: The Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 made possession of a valid passport compulsory for entry into India; the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1936 requires foreigners to register; and the Foreigners Act, 1946 (Section 3) empowers the Central Government to make orders prohibiting, regulating or restricting the entry, presence and departure of foreigners. Immigration functions are administered by the Bureau of Immigration under the Ministry of Home Affairs, while Foreigners Regional Registration Offices (FRROs) handle registration and related services.
static.socioEconomic: Visa and entry decisions affect tourism, business travel, academic and cultural exchange, and perceptions of India as a destination for foreign media and professionals.
static.whyInNews: A Norwegian journalist stated that she was denied entry to India for the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad despite holding a valid visa, and that no reason was communicated to her.
static.wayForward: Greater transparency in visa cancellation and entry-refusal procedures, including written reasons where feasible, and clearer published guidance for journalist visas — balancing national security with India's interest in a free and accessible press environment.
prelimsPointers: Section 3 of the Foreigners Act, 1946 empowers the Central Government to prohibit, regulate or restrict the entry, presence and departure of foreigners.
Immigration at Indian entry points is administered by the Bureau of Immigration under the Ministry of Home Affairs; FRROs handle registration of foreigners.
Holding a valid visa does not create an enforceable right to enter India; the visa can be cancelled and entry refused.
static.mainsAngle: Should India provide written reasons and an accessible review mechanism for visa cancellations and entry refusals, and how do such decisions affect India's international image and media freedom?

static.topic: Freedom of the press and media freedom under the Constitution
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Article 19); rights of citizens versus persons; role of media
static.whatIsIt: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes freedom of the press, though the press is not separately named in the Constitution. This right belongs only to citizens; Article 21 (life and personal liberty), by contrast, is available to all persons, including foreigners.
static.background: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression to citizens, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). In Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court held that freedom of speech includes the freedom to propagate ideas and to circulate information, treating press freedom as implicit in Article 19(1)(a). The Press Council of India is a statutory quasi-judicial body under the Press Council Act, 1978.
static.socioEconomic: Press-freedom assessments and international rankings feed into perceptions of India's openness, with knock-on effects on foreign investment, academic collaboration and soft power.
static.whyInNews: A foreign journalist's denial of entry and visa cancellation has been described by her as 'politically motivated', reviving debate on access for foreign media and the scope of press freedom.
static.wayForward: Publish clear criteria and timelines for journalist visas and accreditation, communicate decisions promptly, and ensure that security considerations are applied through transparent, reviewable procedures.
keyTerms: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)
prelimsPointers: Rights under Article 19 are available only to citizens, whereas Article 21 is available to all persons, including foreigners.
Freedom of the press is not a separate fundamental right; it is read into Article 19(1)(a).
The Press Council of India is a statutory body under the Press Council Act, 1978.
static.mainsAngle: Foreign journalists cannot directly invoke Article 19 in India. Examine how India can reconcile sovereign control over entry with its commitment to a free press and to its international obligations.

static.topic: Press, propaganda and the freedom struggle
static.syllabusNode: Modern Indian History — Freedom Struggle; colonial regulation of the press and institutions
static.whatIsIt: The role of newspapers and the vernacular press in the national movement, and the colonial state's efforts to regulate them — a recurring theme in the history of Indian political mobilisation.
static.background: Key milestones of the freedom struggle include the Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement (1905), Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience and the Dandi March (1930), the Government of India Act 1935, Quit India (1942), the Cabinet Mission (1946), and the Mountbatten Plan leading to the Indian Independence Act 1947. The Indian National Congress was founded by A.O. Hume in 1885.
static.whyInNews: Current debates over media freedom and access for journalists echo colonial-era controls on the press during the freedom struggle.
prelimsPointers: The Indian National Congress was founded by A.O. Hume in 1885.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 created India and Pakistan as dominions.
static.mainsAngle: Nature of mass mobilisation and the role of marginalised voices; colonial legacies in institutions — including the regulation of the press.

prelims: A valid visa does not create an enforceable right to enter India; entry can be refused and a visa cancelled under the Foreigners Act, 1946.
Article 19(1)(a) rights belong only to citizens, so foreign journalists cannot invoke press freedom under it directly; Article 21 covers all persons.
The Bureau of Immigration, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, administers immigration at Indian entry points, while FRROs handle registration of foreigners.

stories.mainsQuestion: A valid visa is not a guarantee of entry into a country. In the light of recent refusals of entry to foreign journalists, examine how India can balance its sovereign control over immigration with the constitutional spirit of a free press and its international image. stories.summary: Indian public-sector firm BEML plans to manufacture tunnel-boring machines, initially smaller units for metro, hydropower, irrigation and water projects, to reduce reliance on Chinese equipment. The Adani Group will finance a copper project in Chile with Codelco, aiming to secure long-term supply for its Mundra smelter as India seeks overseas mineral access. ReNew will invest ₹29,500 crore in Andhra Pradesh for a 2 GW pumped-storage project and a green ammonia and e-fuel facility. Global electric-vehicle sales returned to growth in October, rising 8% to 2.09 million units, led by Europe even as China cooled and US tax-credit support lagged. Separately, the Union Minister inaugurated a promenade at Visakhapatnam port and laid foundation stones for ₹560 crore projects, highlighting the port's maritime and economic potential.
stories.whyItMatters: These developments span industrial self-reliance, critical-mineral security, clean-energy investment, EV demand trends and port infrastructure—key themes for GS-III economy, infrastructure and environment, and GS-II India's external economic engagements.

stories.headline: Finance briefs: RBI transfer norms, private credit, market updates

The RBI published money market operations data for 11 November, showing overnight volumes and weighted average rates, while revised domestic money transfer norms now allow banks to offer cash pay-in and pay-out services subject to transaction limits, customer verification, authentication and monitoring safeguards. Separately, a proposed amendment to the Sarfaesi Act could give private credit funds recovery powers comparable to banks and NBFCs, potentially lowering borrowing costs and widening business funding options. Equity markets were seen opening flat to negative ahead of India's inflation data, with lower crude oil prices supportive; PNB shares hit a 52-week high, Tata Power named Sanjay Banga CEO and posted a Q2 profit jump, and Fairfax was reported to be likely exiting IIFL Finance. static.topic: RBI's money market operations and revised domestic money transfer norms
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: The RBI conducts money market operations to manage liquidity and short-term interest rates; its revised domestic money transfer directions set rules for banks offering cash pay-in/pay-out services.
static.background: RBI was established in 1935, nationalised in 1949, and functions under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (2016), with an inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI (±2%). Tools include repo, reverse repo, Marginal Standing Facility, CRR, SLR and Open Market Operations. The revised money transfer norms prescribe transaction limits, customer verification, authentication and safeguards against unusual transfers.
static.socioEconomic: Affects remittance access, financial inclusion, bank intermediation and cost of funds.
static.whyInNews: RBI released money market operations data for 11 November 2026 and revised domestic money transfer norms allowing banks to offer cash pay-in/pay-out services.
static.wayForward: Strengthen monitoring and customer protection while ensuring smooth liquidity transmission and wider access to formal transfer channels.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
MPC has six members: three RBI including Governor as chair, plus three external; Governor has casting vote.
Inflation target: 4% CPI, band 2–6%, reviewed every five years.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how RBI's liquidity management and payment-transfer regulations balance financial stability, inclusion and customer protection.

static.topic: Proposed Sarfaesi Act amendment for private credit funds
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: The Sarfaesi Act enables secured creditors to enforce security interests without court intervention. A proposed amendment could extend recovery powers to private credit funds, which currently lack powers available to banks and NBFCs.
static.background: Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (Article 79). Bills become law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Money Bills originate only in Lok Sabha (Article 110). The Sarfaesi Act was enacted to help banks and financial institutions recover secured loans; amendments are routed through Parliament.
static.socioEconomic: Could lower borrowing costs, widen business funding options and affect credit recovery efficiency, but raises questions on borrower safeguards.
static.whyInNews: A proposed Sarfaesi Act change is being discussed to give private credit funds more teeth to recover loans.
static.wayForward: Ensure parliamentary scrutiny and balanced safeguards for borrowers while improving recovery mechanisms and credit market depth.
prelimsPointers: No-confidence motion can be moved only in Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in Rajya Sabha lapses on Lok Sabha dissolution only if not yet passed by Lok Sabha.
Money Bills originate only in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can delay but not amend money provisions.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether extending Sarfaesi-type recovery powers to private credit funds will deepen credit markets without weakening borrower protection.

prelims: RBI's revised domestic money transfer directions allow banks to offer cash pay-in/pay-out services with transaction limits, customer verification, authentication and monitoring of unusual transfers.
A proposed amendment to the Sarfaesi Act could extend loan recovery powers to private credit funds, potentially lowering borrowing costs and widening business funding options.

stories.mainsQuestion: The RBI's revised domestic money transfer norms and the proposed Sarfaesi amendment for private credit funds aim to expand formal finance and improve recovery. Examine how these measures balance financial inclusion, customer protection and financial stability.

Taken together, the incidents point to a ceasefire under severe strain and to violence extending beyond Gaza into the occupied West Bank.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the durability of the Gaza ceasefire and the credibility of international humanitarian law on protecting medical facilities and civilians. It also frames India's balancing act between Israel and Palestine — a recurring GS-II International Relations theme.

static.topic: Gaza Ceasefire and the Israel–Hamas Conflict
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — West Asia / Conflict in West Asia
static.whatIsIt: The Israel–Hamas conflict centres on Gaza, a small, densely populated Palestinian coastal territory blockaded since 2007. A ceasefire agreement — described in current reports as about a year old — has been repeatedly strained by strikes and counter-strikes, with each side accusing the other of violations.
static.background: Balfour Declaration 1917; UN Partition Plan (UNGA Resolution 181) 1947; Israel's statehood 1948; the 1967 Six-Day War brought the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza under Israeli occupation; the Oslo Accords of 1993–95 created the Palestinian Authority and divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C; Israel unilaterally withdrew settlers and troops from Gaza in 2005; Hamas took control of Gaza in 2007, followed by blockade; major escalations occurred in 2008–09, 2012, 2014, 2021 and from October 2023.
static.geography: The Gaza Strip borders Israel, Egypt (Rafah crossing) and the Mediterranean Sea; Khan Younis and Rafah lie in the south, where displaced populations have concentrated.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged blockade, repeated displacement and destruction of health infrastructure have left Gaza heavily aid-dependent, with UN agencies warning of famine risk and collapse of basic services.
static.whyInNews: Strikes on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed civilians, with casualty figures reported as four (Anadolu Ajansı) and five (Gaza civil defence, via The Hindu and The Straits Times); Israel says Hamas is regrouping, while Hamas says it remains committed to the ceasefire.
static.wayForward: Sustained ceasefire monitoring, unimpeded humanitarian access, protection of medical facilities, and a credible political track leading to a two-state solution.
prelimsPointers: Nasser Hospital is located in Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
Gaza has been under an Israeli-led blockade since 2007, when Hamas took control of the Strip.
UNRWA (1949) is the UN agency mandated to assist Palestine refugees.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why ceasefires in Gaza have proved fragile, and assess the role of regional mediators and the UN in stabilising them.

static.topic: International Humanitarian Law and Protection of Hospitals
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law and Humanitarian Norms
static.whatIsIt: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), codified chiefly in the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977, regulates conduct in armed conflict through the principles of distinction, proportionality, precaution and military necessity. Medical units, medical personnel and the wounded are specifically protected.
static.background: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 (India is a party) and Additional Protocols I and II of 1977 form the core of IHL; the Fourth Geneva Convention governs the protection of civilians in occupied territory; the Rome Statute of 1998 established the International Criminal Court; the International Court of Justice hears inter-state disputes, including a case filed by South Africa in December 2023 alleging genocide in Gaza.
static.whyInNews: Hospitals in Gaza have repeatedly been struck or forced out of service, raising questions about compliance with IHL obligations to protect medical facilities and civilians.
static.wayForward: Strengthen accountability mechanisms, ensure humanitarian corridors and deconfliction of medical facilities, and reaffirm the obligation to protect civilians in occupied territory.
prelimsPointers: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977 form the core of IHL.
The ICC, established by the Rome Statute (1998), sits at The Hague; the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN, also at The Hague.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether existing international legal mechanisms are adequate to enforce IHL in contemporary asymmetric conflicts.

static.topic: India's West Asia Policy and the Two-State Solution
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World / India's West Asia Policy
static.whatIsIt: India's West Asia policy balances historic support for the Palestinian cause with a deepening strategic and economic partnership with Israel — a deliberate approach often described as de-hyphenation, dealing with Israel and Palestine on separate tracks.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but full diplomatic relations began only in 1992; India was the first non-Arab state to recognise the PLO (1974) and has consistently voted for Palestinian rights at the UN; ties with Gulf states rest on energy, remittances and a large expatriate workforce; the I2U2 grouping and the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (announced at the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi) reflect newer connectivity interests.
static.geography: West Asia and the Gulf include energy chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb; the proposed corridor route runs India–Arabian Sea–Gulf–Israel–Europe.
static.socioEconomic: India imports a substantial share of its crude oil from West Asia and hosts a large expatriate workforce there; regional instability affects energy prices, shipping and remittances.
static.whyInNews: Renewed Israeli strikes in Gaza and continuing violence in the West Bank keep the conflict live, testing India's balancing diplomacy and its stated support for a two-state solution.
static.wayForward: Continue principled support for a two-state solution, humanitarian assistance to Palestinians, and diversified energy and connectivity partnerships across the region.
prelimsPointers: India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992.
India was the first non-Arab country to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organisation (1974).
static.mainsAngle: India's West Asia policy must reconcile historical solidarity with Palestine and a strategic partnership with Israel. Critically examine.

prelims: Gaza civil defence reported five killed in a strike on a hospital in southern Gaza, while Anadolu Ajansı reported four killed at Nasser Hospital — casualty figures in the conflict are frequently contested and revised.
Israel said it had stepped up attacks because Hamas was trying to regroup and refill its arsenal; Hamas said it remained committed to the year-old ceasefire and accused Israel of undermining it.
Israeli forces shot dead a 14-year-old in the West Bank, according to Palestinian officials; the Israeli military said it acted to thwart stone-hurling and terrorist attacks.
Nasser Hospital, the site of the reported strike, is located in Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
stories.mainsQuestion: The repeated targeting of medical facilities in Gaza and continuing violence in the West Bank raise serious questions about compliance with international humanitarian law. Discuss, with reference to the role of the UN and regional mediators, and evaluate India's position on the Israel–Palestine question.

stories.headline: FIR against Mamata Banerjee over SIR protest remarks; brother joins rebel camp
stories.summary: An FIR has been registered against former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee over remarks she allegedly made at a protest against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, in which she is reported to have told a minority community that its safety depended on her and to have dismissed the BJP's statements as misleading. In a separate development, Banerjee skipped the Bhai Phonta celebrations at her residence, and her brother joined a rebel camp, praising Suvendu Adhikari. While some supporters gathered at her residence, most of her erstwhile loyalists were conspicuously absent. Taken together, the two developments point to simultaneous legal and organisational pressure on the TMC leadership.
stories.whyItMatters: The story sits at the intersection of three recurring GS-II themes: the ECI's power to order electoral-roll revision, the limits of political speech under Article 19(2), and party discipline under the Tenth Schedule.

perspectives.take: The FIR report frames the episode as a legal-consequences story — a national, Delhi-datelined account of an alleged communal appeal at an SIR protest, reported without editorial comment on the merits.
The Kolkata-city report frames the Bhai Phonta absence and the brother's move to the rebel camp as evidence of internal erosion in the TMC, with a local party-politics lens.

static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Elections, Electoral Reforms, Constitutional Bodies (Election Commission of India)
static.whatIsIt: A door-to-door, constituency-wide revision of electoral rolls ordered by the ECI under its plenary powers under Article 324 read with Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, in which existing electors must re-establish eligibility rather than only additions and deletions being made.
static.background: The ECI has conducted intensive revisions of rolls earlier; a full SIR was carried out in Bihar in 2025 ahead of the Assembly election, and the Commission has since announced similar exercises in other States. Political parties have contested the process before the Commission and in courts.
static.geography: West Bengal — the protest in the news was held against the SIR; SIR-type exercises have been ordered in several States, including Bihar.
static.socioEconomic: Roll revision affects the voting rights and welfare-linked documentation of migrants, the poor and minority groups; opposition parties allege disproportionate exclusion of such electors.
static.whyInNews: The FIR against Mamata Banerjee arose from remarks allegedly made at a protest against the SIR in West Bengal.
static.wayForward: Transparent, publicly auditable revision with published draft rolls, clearly stated deletion criteria, an accessible claims-and-objections machinery and time-bound disposal of appeals.
prelimsPointers: Electoral rolls are prepared by the ECI under Article 324 read with the RP Act, 1950; the ECI is a constitutional body.
SIR requires existing electors to re-verify eligibility and is distinct from the routine summary revision of rolls.
Deletions can be challenged through claims and objections and further appeals before designated electoral authorities.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the ECI's power to order a Special Intensive Revision is adequately balanced by procedural safeguards and judicial review.

static.topic: Reasonable restrictions on speech: communal appeals and religious sentiment
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Fundamental Rights (Article 19), Criminal Law, Model Code of Conduct
static.whatIsIt: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), including public order, decency or morality, and incitement to an offence. Sections 196, 299 and 302 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (successors to IPC Sections 153A, 295A and 505) penalise promoting enmity between groups and deliberate acts intended to outrage religious feelings.
static.background: The Supreme Court has held that speech must bear a proximate nexus to public disorder before it can be restricted, notably in Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989) and Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). The Model Code of Conduct bars election appeals on the ground of religion or caste.
static.socioEconomic: Communal appeals and bloc-vote consolidation affect social harmony and the level playing field in elections.
static.whyInNews: An FIR was registered against Mamata Banerjee over alleged communal remarks made at an SIR protest.
static.wayForward: Prompt, impartial and uniform enforcement of penal law and the Model Code of Conduct across parties, supported by reasoned orders and speedy trial.
prelimsPointers: Article 19(2) grounds include public order, decency or morality, and incitement to an offence.
IPC Sections 153A and 295A correspond to BNS Sections 196 and 299 respectively.
The Model Code of Conduct is not a statute; it is enforced by the Election Commission of India.
static.mainsAngle: Where should the line between political speech and communal incitement be drawn? Discuss with reference to Article 19(2) and recent enforcement practice.

static.topic: Anti-defection law and inner-party dissent
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Parliament and State Legislatures, Tenth Schedule, Political Parties
static.whatIsIt: The Tenth Schedule (inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment, 1985) disqualifies a legislator who voluntarily gives up membership of a party or votes or abstains against a party whip; the 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the exemption for a split by one-third of a legislature party's members.
static.background: Enacted to curb the 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' culture of frequent floor-crossing. Disqualification petitions are decided by the Speaker or Chairman, and the decision is subject to judicial review on limited grounds as held in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992).
static.socioEconomic: The law strengthens party discipline but is criticised for curbing legislators' freedom of expression and weakening accountability to constituents.
static.whyInNews: Mamata Banerjee's brother joining a rebel camp and praising a rival leader points to factionalism within the TMC; the Tenth Schedule governs the position of legislators in such situations.
static.wayForward: Consider independent adjudication of defection cases and limiting the whip to confidence and money bills, as suggested by the Law Commission's 170th Report and various parliamentary committee recommendations.
prelimsPointers: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985; the one-third split exemption was removed by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003.
Only a merger with another party supported by two-thirds of a legislature party's members is protected from disqualification.
The Speaker's or Chairman's decision on disqualification is subject to judicial review on limited grounds.
static.mainsAngle: Does the anti-defection law undermine representative democracy? Evaluate in the light of inner-party dissent and factionalism.

prelims: An FIR was registered against former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee over alleged communal remarks made during a protest against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
SIR is an ECI-ordered, door-to-door revision of electoral rolls carried out under Article 324 read with the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
Promoting enmity between groups on grounds of religion is punishable under BNS Section 196 (earlier IPC Section 153A); communal appeals in elections are barred by the Model Code of Conduct.
The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) disqualifies defecting legislators; the one-third split exemption was removed by the 91st Amendment, 2003.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls has become a flashpoint between the Election Commission and political parties. Examine the constitutional basis of the ECI's power to order an SIR and the procedural safeguards needed to ensure that roll revision does not disenfranchise genuine electors.

onThisDay.title: Bhola Cyclone
onThisDay.description: The 1970 Bhola cyclone made landfall on the coast of East Pakistan, becoming the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The disaster killed an estimated 300,000–500,000 people and deepened the political crisis that preceded the creation of Bangladesh.
